## Grammar

Basic word order is free (no basic order of subject, object and verb); it has prepositions. In the noun phrase: possessor before the possessed; noun before the adjective; demonstrative before the noun; noun before the numeral; noun before the relative clause. Overall it is head-initial.
It has a definite article before the noun, no indefinite article, no case marking on nouns, no alignment marking (subject and object are not told apart by form), singular, dual and plural, no gender or noun classes.
Verbs mark future, perfective and progressive; there are no evidentials. Negation uses a negator after the verb; yes/no questions use a final question particle. Verbs do not agree with their arguments.
Other features: pronouns can be dropped; an inclusive/exclusive 'we' distinction; adjectives that behave like verbs; a bound causative; no passive; question words left in place; a decimal counting base; a 'have' verb for possession.
Measured morphology: 9 live grammatical markers, mean bondedness 1.2 (0 free word … 3 fused), 12 paradigm cells, 3 of them with allomorphy.

### Grammar sketch

Built from the typology and the live markers above (planet/language/sentences.py); where the engine tracks no marker for a construction, the form is the word such markers commonly grow from, and the text says so. Examples are glossed by the Leipzig rules (abbreviations under Sample sentences).

**Number.** Nouns mark number: plural: a suffix that fuses with some stems (ni˦, from 'all'); dual: a separate word after the noun (ju˦, from 'two').

**Case.** Nouns have no case marking. Subject and object are not marked apart: word order tells them. Place and company are said with the plain words 'in' (nu˨), 'at' (ʘe˦ᵑǃ̬u˦), 'with' (jo˨) as adpositions.

**Gender and noun classes.** There is no gender or noun class.

**Tense and aspect.** Verbs mark tense and aspect. Perfect (PRF): a clitic before the verb (pe˦, from 'finish'); future (FUT): a clitic before the verb (i˦zi˦, from 'come'); progressive (PROG): a separate word before the verb (tu˦mo˦, from 'sit'). Unmarked: past, habitual (left to context).

‘(it) is going’

**Mood and evidentiality.** No evidential or mood marker is live; statements are unmarked.

**Person agreement.** Verbs do not agree with the subject.

**Negation.** Negation is a suffix (be˦, from 'nothing').

| *ᵑǀi˦da˦* | *mi˦ǁ̬ʼi˦ǃ̬ʰe˦-be˦* | *le˦le˦=ja˦ʘ̬ʼi˦bi˨mi˦ri˦* |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1SG | drink-NEG | DEF=milk |

‘I do not drink the milk.’ (sentence 6 below)

**Questions.** Yes/no questions use a particle at the end of the clause. Question words stay where the questioned phrase would stand: who su˦n̪e˦, what ʘʰa˦ǁ̬u˦we˦, where ɭe˦, when ʈo˦, how pa˦.

| *ǂʰa˦bu˦* | *n̪o˦je˦ɳu˦* | *le˦le˦=tju˦bi˨.ᵑǁ̬a˦ɡo˦* | *i˦me˦* |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 2SG | hear | DEF=thunder | Q |

‘Do you hear the thunder?’ (sentence 4 below)

| *le˦le˦=je˦ǀ̬u˦* | *i˦zi˦zu˦ǂ̬ʼu˦* | *ʘʰa˦ǁ̬u˦we˦* |
| --- | --- | --- |
| DEF=child | bring | what |

‘What does the child bring?’ (sentence 5 below)

**Commands.** There is no imperative marker: a command is the bare verb stem, with no subject and no subject or tense marker.

| *ju˦mu˦bi˦* | *le˦le˦=re˦* |
| --- | --- |
| eat | DEF=fish |

‘Eat the fish!’ (sentence 12 below)

**Possession.** The possessor stands before the possessed noun, with no marker. 'Having' is said with a 'have' verb ('my mother has a boat').

| *le˦le˦=ri˦lja˦ni˦* | *u˦wi˦* |
| --- | --- |
| DEF=man | dog |

‘the man's dog’

| *ᵑǀi˦da˦* | *ma˦ma˦* | *ʘu˦* | *e˦* |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1SG | mother | have | boat |

‘My mother has a boat.’ (sentence 7 below)

**Relative clauses.** Relative clause after the noun, introduced by the word for 'that' (as English that and German der grew from a pointing word).

| *le˦le˦=ᵑǁa˦ɡi˦ɡa˦* | *lo˦ja˦lu˦jo˦* | *ma˦bo˦mo˦* |
| --- | --- | --- |
| DEF=woman | REL | dance |

‘the woman who dances’

**Copula.** There is no copula: a predicate noun stands beside its subject. Adjectives behave like verbs: 'the water is cold' is said as 'the water colds', with the verb's markers.

| *lo˦ja˦lu˦jo˦* | *ri˦lja˦ni˦* | *e˨hu˨* |
| --- | --- | --- |
| that | man | merchant |

‘That man is a merchant.’ (sentence 9 below)

| *le˦le˦=ja˦ʘ̬ʼi˦bi˨* | *ku˦ro˦ɡi˦* |
| --- | --- |
| DEF=water | cold |

‘the water is cold’

**Pronouns.** 'We' has two forms: inclusive ʘa˨ǂ̬ʰa˦bu˦ (you and I, the hearer among us) and exclusive ʘa˨ (we, but not you).

| *ʘa˨ǂ̬ʰa˦bu˦* |
| --- |
| 1PL.INCL |

‘we (you included)’

| *ʘa˨* |
| --- |
| 1PL.EXCL |

‘we (not you)’

| *ʘa˨ǂ̬ʰa˦bu˦* | *ju˦mu˦bi˦* | *le˦le˦=re˦* |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1PL.INCL | eat | DEF=fish |

‘We (you and I) eat the fish.’ (sentence 13 below)

**Giving (two objects).** Double object: theme and recipient both unmarked.

| *le˦le˦=ᵑǁa˦ɡi˦ɡa˦* | *ʘʰi˦ǁ̬i˦ʁa˨* | *re˦* | *le˦le˦=je˦ǀ̬u˦* |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| DEF=woman | give | fish | DEF=child |

‘The woman gives the child a fish.’ (sentence 11 below)

**Numerals.** Counting is decimal: numbers above ten are built from ten and the units. Twenty is ne˦u˦ and a hundred is ja˦.

| *ŋʷo˦lo˦na˦* |
| --- |
| 11 |

‘11 = 10 + 1 ('ten' and 'one')’

| *ᵑʘi˦na˦* |
| --- |
| 15 |

‘15 = 10 + 5 ('ten' and 'five')’

| *na˦ɭe˦ɡe˦* |
| --- |
| 30 |

‘30 = 10 × 3 ('ten' and 'three')’

**Linking clauses.** Complement clauses stand bare, with no complementizer.

| *le˦le˦=ri˦lja˦ni˦* | *n̪o˦je˦ǂ̬ʼu˦* | *le˦le˦=ju˦wi˦* | *n̪i˦ɡo˦ʁʷu˦* |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| DEF=man | say | DEF=dog | sleep |

‘The man says that the dog sleeps.’ (sentence 14 below)

**Topic and focus.** There is no topic marker, but the free word order puts the topic first.

| *le˦le˦=re˦* | *le˦le˦=ri˦lja˦ni˦* | *ju˦mu˦bi˦* |
| --- | --- | --- |
| DEF=fish | DEF=man | eat |

‘The fish, the man eats it.’ (sentence 15 below)

**Demonstratives.** Demonstratives count two distances: 'this' e˦bu˦zi˦ (near) and 'that' lo˦ja˦lu˦jo˦ (far).

| *e˦bu˦zi˦* | *u˦wi˦* |
| --- | --- |
| this | dog |

‘this dog’

| *lo˦ja˦lu˦jo˦* | *u˦wi˦* |
| --- | --- |
| that | dog |

‘that dog’

**Comparison.** An 'exceed' comparison: 'A is big, exceeds B', with the verb for 'climb' (as Yoruba ju 'exceed', Thai kwaa 'cross over').

| *le˦le˦=ri˦lja˦ni˦* | *ka˦ne˦ɡe˦* | *kʷe˨bo˦ǂ̬ʰa˦* | *le˦le˦=ju˦wi˦* |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| DEF=man | big | exceed | DEF=dog |

‘The man is bigger than the dog.’ (sentence 16 below)

| dough | i˦ɖi˦ǀ̬u˦wa˦ʘ̬ʼe˦ | idigǀuwagpx'e | flour, flow | \*iʈiǀʰu 'flour' (the elf proto-language, 20 kyr) → FLOUR + WATER = 'dough' (7.5) |
| shore | pe˦nja˦ʘ̬ʼi˦ | penyagpx'i | end (of space), flow, salt | \*pakine 'end (of space)' (the elf proto-language, 20 kyr) → 'end (of space)' > 'edge' (18.5) → EDGE + SEA = 'shore' (1) |
| … | | | | 4 more |

## Names of people and places

**Naming tradition.** Given names are a short sentence about the birth run together (as Yoruba *Babatunde* 'father has returned'); the byname is the mother's name in the genitive with 'son' or 'daughter'. The tradition goes back to the elf proto-language.

| name | IPA | meaning | | etymology |
\|---\|---\|---\|---\|---\|
| **Yegǀuwizi** | /je˦ǀ̬u˦wi˦zi˦/ | 'the child came' | old | Yegǀuwizi 'the child came': yegǀu 'child' + izizu 'come'; an old name, coined in d551 4.0 kyr ago as Yegǀuizi |
| **Letulina** | /le˦du˦li˦n̪a˦/ | 'the people sing' | old | Letulina 'the people sing': netuwi 'people' + linaṇu 'sing'; an old name, coined in d551 4.0 kyr ago as Netulina |
| **Mamaga** | /ma˦ma˦ɡa˦/ | 'mother laughed' | old | Mamaga 'mother laughed': mama 'mother' + ka 'laugh'; an old name, coined in d551 4.0 kyr ago as Mamaka |
| **Konubele** | /ko˨nu˦be˦le˦/ | 'the war is over' | new | Konubele 'the war is over': konubibi 'war' + peleṇu 'finish'; coined from today's words |
| **Tiyunao** | /ʈi˦ju˦na˦o˦/ | 'the sun rose' | new | Tiyunao 'the sun rose': tiwyubu 'sun' + nao 'rise'; coined from today's words |
| **Yangǀuziza** | /ja˦ᵑǀ̬u˦zi˦za˦/ | 'God knows' | new | Yangǀuziza 'God knows': yangǀu 'god' + siza 'know'; coined from today's words |
| **Yegǀuwizi Seḻuletu** | /je˦ǀ̬u˦wi˦zi˦ se˦ɻu˦le˦du˦/ | 'the child came, son of the people sing' | matronymic | the mother's name Letulina + seḻu 'son' (compounded: the language has no genitive marker) |
| **Letulina Sebamama** | /le˦du˦li˦n̪a˦ se˦ba˦ma˦ma˦/ | 'the people sing, daughter of mother laughed' | matronymic | the mother's name Mamaga + sebazi 'daughter' (compounded: the language has no genitive marker) |

**Settlements.** **Miletu** /mi˦le˦du˦/ (town, 7,312): 'Letulina's fence'; from fence (worn to a suffix), founded 4.0 kyr ago; **Leduwezo** /ɭe˦ɖu˦we˦zo˦/ (town, 6,091): 'the low market'; from market, founded 0.6 kyr ago; **Leduzino** /ɭe˦ɖu˦zi˦n̪o˦/ (town, 5,144): 'the old market'; from market, founded 0.6 kyr ago.

## Gods and liturgy

**Faith.** The sky faith of the earliest hill giants of the east of Ratal, founded 300 kyr ago ago, held by 27 languages.

| god | name | IPA | meaning | the same name elsewhere |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| god of sky and storm | **Kuyomwobubi** | /ku˦jo˦mʷo˦bu˦bi˨/ | 'roof of the world' | Kuyomwobu (elf 16), Kuyomwubi (drow 1), Kuwomwobi (drow 2) ... |
| god of fire and forest | **ǃHyoṇugǀu** | /ǃʰjo˦ɳu˦ǀ̬u˦/ | 'the one who burns' | ǃHiyinigǀi (elf 16), ǃHiyoṇusu (drow 1), ǃHiyoṇurru (drow 2) ... |
| god of hearth and ancestors | **Sinogǁ'ogǀu** | /si˦n̪o˦ǁ̬ʼo˦ǀ̬u˦/ | 'the old one' | Hinoǁ'osu (drow 1), Inoǁ'orru (drow 2), Inogǁ'ogǀu (elf 28) |
| god of hunt and fertility | **Lyemebo** | /ɭje˦me˦bo˦/ | 'chief of the hunt' | Ḷiyimebe (elf 16), Liyimebo (drow 1), Ḷiyimebo (drow 2) ... |

How the first name came about: 'sky-father' (a kin title (the old name avoided); it replaced the old name tuzubulu 'king of the sky') in d24, 19 kyr ago.

**Liturgy.** The faith's rites are kept in the hill giant speech of hill giant 1 as it was 4.5 kyr ago ago, frozen since (as Latin, Sanskrit or Ge'ez are).

Built from this language's own words, word order, markers and agreement (planet/language/sentences.py). Each has the form line (‘-’ an affix boundary, ‘=’ a clitic boundary), a morpheme-by-morpheme gloss, the free translation, then the whole sentence in IPA (after the simple joining rules: a glide between two vowels, a nasal taking the place of a following stop) and in the book spelling. Nothing here is attested speech; it is what the grammar data implies.

## Texts

Each sentence in four lines: the book spelling, the IPA with its morph breaks, the gloss, and the English.

### A fable: The Bird and the Fish

One fixed short fable, told in every language as August Schleicher told his in Proto-Indo-European (1868), so that the same text shows what sound change and grammar change did. English: A bird sat in a tree. The bird saw a fish in the water. The bird said: “Come! I will give you a good seed.” The fish said: “I do not eat seeds. You will eat me.” The fish did not come. The bird ate the seed.

### A myth: What the gods hold (the sky faith of the earliest hill giants of the east of Ratal)

What the faith data holds, told in this language: each god's domain, the high god's gift, the foods forbidden because they belong to a god, and the invocation. Nothing is added: the run records no creation story or deeds.
